# Multilingual voicebot

<p class="sx-lede">Technology reached millions. Language left many behind.</p>

Banking apps and government scheme websites mostly speak English. I built a voicebot that lets someone ask a money question out loud in their own language and hear the answer spoken back. The first version, in 2023 (Grade 9), included a phone-call path. In 2025 I rebuilt it on Telegram, self-hosted on Google Cloud, with a dashboard showing which languages and modes people used.

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">The problem</p>

## Information exists. It just is not in the right language, or the right form

Many people who would benefit most from a savings scheme, an insurance product or a simple explanation of interest are more comfortable speaking than typing, and speaking Kannada, Tamil or Hindi rather than English. I spent time around researchers at IISc working on exactly this question: how AI could make reliable financial information easier to reach for rural and suburban customers in their own languages.

That institutional work is [Project SAATHI](https://sites.google.com/iisc.ac.in/saathi/technical-architecture?authuser=0){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}, an IISc-led initiative funded by a Grand Challenges grant, [Enabling Equal Finance Access for Rural Customers in India](https://gcgh.grandchallenges.org/grant/enabling-equal-finance-access-rural-customers-india){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}. It gave me the problem. I was not a named member of its core team or of the grant; the voicebot on this page is my own independent prototype.
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">What I built</p>

## One pipeline for any language: listen, understand, answer, speak

::: {.sx-two}

::: {}
A user sends a voice note or a text message to the Telegram bot. The bot works out which language it is in, answers briefly in that same language, and replies with both text and a spoken version. The user never has to pick a language from a menu.

I wrote the backend in Python and deployed it as a serverless function on Google Cloud, with the infrastructure defined as code so it can be rebuilt from scratch. Speech recognition and the answers come from OpenAI's models; the spoken reply uses Google Cloud Text-to-Speech, which has voices for Indian languages. An earlier WhatsApp version started from a public tutorial.

Each interaction's language and mode (voice or text) are recorded in a database, and a small web dashboard turns them into weekly patterns.
:::

<ol class="sx-flow" aria-label="How a question is answered">
<li><b>Ask</b><span>A voice note or text message on Telegram</span></li>
<li><b>Transcribe and detect</b><span>Speech becomes text, and the language is identified</span></li>
<li><b>Answer</b><span>A short reply, at most 250 words, in the same language</span></li>
<li><b>Speak</b><span>Text-to-speech in a voice for that language</span></li>
<li><b>Reply and count</b><span>Text and audio sent back; language and mode logged for the dashboard</span></li>
</ol>

:::
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">What it showed</p>

## People chose text more often than voice

On the dashboard, about 23% of interactions are voice and 77% text, and the most-used languages are Kannada, Tamil, Telugu, Hindi and English. The bot was designed around voice, yet most messages were typed. These counts include my own testing and cannot be separated from it, so they show how the bot was used, not how many people used it.

<blockquote class="sx-pull">
<p>Was language really the barrier?</p>
<p>The voicebot assumed it was. That assumption became the starting point for my research with security guards at IISc, which measured what else stands between people and financial decisions.</p>
</blockquote>
:::
